title: Service Criticality and Capacity Prioritization Guidelines
author: Nora Patel
content:
Summary
This guideline defines how Redwood SRE assesses service criticality, allocates capacity, and enforces error-budget-driven prioritization. It combines SLO policy, capacity hedging, incident escalation priorities, and operational tooling patterns into a single decision framework for on-call teams and product owners. Use this document to: determine capacity pre-commitments, run surge prioritization, and decide which services receive emergency capacity in constrained scenarios.

Context and goals
- Objective: ensure customer-facing and revenue-significant features meet latency and availability commitments while minimizing waste across the GPU fleet and reserved pools.
- Scope: applies to all services that serve production inference traffic (hosted API, dedicated, private control plane) and platform dependencies that affect SLOs (routing, auth, billing).
- Not in scope: internal dev/test workloads, ephemeral CI jobs (see infra-standards for CI quotas).

Definitions
1) Service criticality tier (used for prioritization decisions)
   - Tier A (critical): Revenue-facing APIs and model endpoints used by >1M monthly requests or with enterprise SLAs. Examples: /v1/generate, dedicated inference gateways.
   - Tier B (important): Features with user-facing impact but lower revenue sensitivity or lower scale (e.g., internal embeddings used by search).
   - Tier C (non-critical): Experimental features, analytics-only jobs, internal tooling.

2) SLO constructs
   - Availability SLO: % of successful responses within defined HTTP code set and within latency target.
   - Latency SLO: p99 / p95 token latency measured on production traffic after warm caches.
   - Error budget: 1 - SLO over a rolling window (typically 30 days). Error budget burn = observed violations / budget.

Service criticality table (summary view)
| Column | Description | Sample threshold |
|-------|-------------|------------------|
| Tier | Criticality label | A / B / C |
| Ownership | Primary product and SRE owner | product: embeddings; sre: team-gamma |
| Core SLOs | Primary SLOs that drive capacity decisions | availability 99.95% / latency p99 < 300ms |
| Capacity policy | Pre-commit / hedging strategy | reserved 4x baseline for Tier A |

Policy: How capacity commitments are decided
- Baseline RPS calculation: for each service, compute 7-day median RPS and 95th percentile of hourly peaks. Baseline = max(7-day median, 95th-peak * 0.6).
- Headroom multiplier by tier: Tier A = 4.0, Tier B = 2.0, Tier C = 1.2. These are applied to baseline to determine reserved capacity on Dedicated pools or autoscaler targets in hosted regions.
- Cost-optimization review cadence: quarterly for Tier A and B, biannual for Tier C. Reviews must include model quantization plans and caching strategies.

Error budget prioritization (decision ladder)
When error budget is burning, apply the following prioritized actions in order (do not skip earlier steps unless explicitly approved by SRE lead):
1) Throttle non-critical background traffic (Tier C) via rate-limiters and global traffic shaping.
2) Enable aggressive prefix/KV cache usage and bypass model cold starts where possible.
3) Engage model-variant fallback (quantized / smaller models) for non-enterprise customers.
4) If error budget remains negative for >6 hours, open emergency capacity arbitration and consider reassigning reserved nodes from Tier C services.
5) For sustained critical burns (>24 hours), trigger product escalation: reduce feature flags for non-SLA customers and notify sales/customer-success for impacted enterprise tenants.

Runbook: Capacity emergency triage (ordered steps)
1) Identify the scope: runredwood query:
   redwoodctl metrics query --service <service> --range 60m --metrics requests,errors,latency
2) Check SLO dashboard: Grafana link (dash:prod/service-slo) and error-budget burn graph.
3) If burn rate > 3x expected and p99 latency > 2x target, notify on-call and create incident with impact level P1/P2.
4) Apply short-term mitigations:
   a) Route non-enterprise traffic to fallback region: redwoodctl route set --service <s> --region fallback-west --filter "!enterprise"
   b) Scale up dedicated pool: redwoodctl capacity allocate --pool dedicated-g1 --count +2 --reason "emergency hedging"
   c) Update autoscaler policy to more aggressive scaling: kubectl apply -f autoscaler-emergency.yaml
5) Re-evaluate every 15 minutes until error budget burn rate reduces below threshold.

Incident review and capacity ownership checklist
- Evidence to collect (during incident): timeline of scaling events, autoscaler logs, GPU utilization heatmaps, kernel-level stalls, model KV cache hit rates, and routing traces.
- Minimum metadata to attach to post-incident review: owner, rollback window, capacity decisions, and cost delta for emergency capacity.
- Review cadence: incidents impacting Tier A SLOs require a blameless postmortem within 72 hours and a capacity remediation plan in the first retro.

Operational tooling recommendations
- Metrics and dashboards: Prometheus + Cortex for long retention, Grafana dashboards per-service with the following panels: requests, pct-iles latency, error-rate, CPU/GPU utilization, queue length, kv-cache-hit.
- Alerts (recommended thresholds):
   - service_slo_error_budget_burn_rate > 1.0 for 1h -> SEV3
   - p99_latency > p99_target * 1.5 for 30m -> SEV2
   - gpu_utilization > 88% for 10m and queue_length > 50 -> SEV2
   - routing_5xx_rate > 0.5% for 10m -> SEV2
- Integrations: PagerDuty for on-call, Slack incident channel automation, and runbook links embedded in alerts. Use the internal tool redwood-alerts to attach runbook pointers automatically.

Capacity prioritization algorithm (for automated arbitration)
- Input signals: SLO priority score (weighted by tier and enterprise impact), current error budget remaining, cost per vGPU-hour, and region redundancy margin.
- Simplified scoring formula (example):
   priority_score = (tier_weight * SLO_score) + (enterprise_weight * enterprise_qps_share) - (cost_weight * vgpu_cost)
   where tier_weight: A=100, B=60, C=20; enterprise_weight is proportion of requests from paid customers; cost_weight normalizes to dollars/hour.
- Use-case: when total demand exceeds capacity by X% (configurable), automated arbiter will: 1) reallocate up to configured soft-reserve from Tier C with lowest score, 2) apply throttles to flagged low-priority routes, 3) propose manual approval to allocate paid reserved nodes.

Capacity change governance and audit trail
- Any manual reallocation of reserved capacity must be recorded in the capacity-change ledger (redwoodctl capacity log --record) with the following fields: service, from_pool, to_pool, node_count, rationale, approver.
- Audit retention: capacity logs retained 13 months. Capacity changes tied to incidents are included in postmortem artifacts.

Pre-deployment checklist for new services (capacity & SLO readiness)
1) Define primary SLOs (availability and latency) and target error budget.
2) Provide 14-day synthetic traffic profile or representative replay.
3) Declare criticality tier and justify from product owner.
4) Estimate baseline RPS and recommended headroom.
5) Register service on capacity dashboard and set initial autoscaler policies.

Example artifacts and snippets
- Sample autoscaler override (YAML):
  apiVersion: autoscaling.redwood.io/v1
  kind: InferenceAutoscaler
  metadata:
    name: embeddings-autoscaler
  spec:
    minReplicas: 3
    maxReplicas: 30
    scalePolicy:
      cpu: 0.7
      queueLength: 20
    emergencyOverrides:
      p99Latency: 300ms
      enabled: true

- Capacity query example (CLI):
  redwoodctl capacity plan --service embeddings --window 7d --percentile 95 --output json

Ownership and escalation paths
- Primary owner: SRE team assigned in service metadata (sre-owner label).
- Secondary owner: Product manager or engineering manager for the owning team.
- Capacity triage contact list: on-call, capacity-allocator, infra-ops. If on-call is unreachable escalate to SRE lead and product director.

Audit and continuous improvement
- Quarterly exercises: simulate 10–30% sudden cross-region traffic spikes and validate arbitration behavior. Record lessons and refine headroom multipliers.
- Monthly SLO sprint: product and SRE run a 2-week review of service-level regressions and capacity rebalancing proposals.

Appendix: quick links and runbooks
- SLO dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/prod/service-slo

Contact and feedback
If you have questions about applying this guideline to a specific product, email sre-policy@redwood.ai or open an RFC in the eng-sre team wiki.
